beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The Tao of OMIS explores love without treating another person as a completed answer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its standalone speculative triptych begins with finite people in a habitable dusk belt.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Their attraction opens a question about influence, difference, and a future left unclaimed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The larger realms preserve that intimate question while changing its scale.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its vocabulary distinguishes a relationship's influence from quietly removing another person's possible futures.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The stories keep that distinction embodied in people who can disagree and change.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Mara and Sio live within a habitable belt between intense heat and cold.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Their world depends on practical forms of care, transport, and ecological attention.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The relationship begins among finite people with different habits and responsibilities.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Attraction does not settle how much one life may organize another.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The setting gives dependence a material presence before the story expands its scale.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its intimacy matters because an uncertain future cannot be replaced by perfect agreement.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The later spirals bring observers and more powerful realms into the inquiry.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Greater resolution does not automatically provide a better understanding of another life.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book distinguishes care from a convergence that quietly narrows what someone may become.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its complementary modes are not fixed genders or permanent kinds of person.
